issues.legal_issue: A state law establishing an industrial development corporation and providing for land acquisition is within the State Legislature’s competence when its true purpose is industrial development and the corporation acts as a government agency rather than as a trading corporation.
material_facts: The law was enacted to secure the orderly establishment, growth and development of industries through industrial areas and industrial estates.
The corporation was created to carry out that purpose, with members nominated by the State Government and public bodies, and it was subject to government policy directions.
The corporation developed industrial areas and estates, provided infrastructure and facilities, constructed buildings, and made land and buildings available to industrial undertakings.
The State could acquire land for the law’s purposes and transfer it to the corporation for development.

The corporation’s receipts from land, buildings and rents funded its statutory functions; it was not established by shareholders to conduct business for profit, and its assets and liabilities would pass to the State upon dissolution.
The industrial development at issue did not concern industries reserved to the Union under the constitutional entries discussed by the Court.
issues.conclusion: The corporation was not a trading corporation, and the law’s pith and substance was industrial development, including acquisition of land for that purpose. The law was validly enacted by the State Legislature.
issues.legal_principle: The pith and substance and true intent of legislation determine its validity. Industrial development falls within Entry 24 of the State List, subject to Entries 7 and 52 of the Union List; acquisition of land falls within Entry 42 of the Concurrent List. The corporation’s powers and receipts did not make it a trading corporation because its role was to carry out the State’s industrial-development purpose, not to engage in commercial buying and selling. The Court also held that the corporation was not a government company under section 617 of the Companies Act, 1956, and noted section 616 in considering that Act’s application. No earlier cases are relied on in the supplied judgment.

rule.if: constitutional_challenge_to_state_industrial_development_law and primary_purpose_is_industrial_development and corporation_acts_for_government_purpose and land_acquisition_serves_that_purpose and industries_are_not_union_reserved

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_state_indust: The proceeding challenges the validity of a state law that establishes an industrial development body and provides for related land acquisition.
predicates.primary_purpose_is_industrial_developmen: The law’s principal purpose is the orderly establishment, growth or development of industries.
predicates.corporation_acts_for_government_purpose: The development body is controlled or directed by public authorities and performs functions to carry out the law’s public purpose rather than to conduct a shareholder-owned profit-making business.
predicates.land_acquisition_serves_that_purpose: Land is acquired for the development body or related public development work in furtherance of industrial development.
predicates.industries_are_not_union_reserved: The industries addressed by the law do not fall within the categories assigned to the Union under the constitutional provisions considered by the Court.

issues.definition: When a constitutional challenge concerns a state industrial-development law, the law has an industrial-development purpose, its corporation carries out a government purpose, acquisition serves that purpose, and the industries are not union-reserved, the law is within legislative competence.

issues.legal_issue: A special state law providing for land acquisition to develop planned industrial areas and estates is not procedurally discriminatory merely because it uses a different procedure from the general acquisition law, which provides for acquisition for companies.
material_facts: The challenged law provided its own procedure for acquiring land for industrial areas, industrial estates and other purposes furthering its objectives.
Acquisition under the challenged law was by the State for public purposes, while acquisition under the general law for companies was at a company’s instance and for its benefit.
The challenged law aimed to create planned industrial areas and estates and to promote the orderly development and dispersal of industries.
issues.conclusion: The two acquisition procedures applied in dissimilar situations and circumstances, so the difference between them did not amount to procedural discrimination.
issues.legal_principle: A special law directed to the growth, development and organisation of industries may have its own acquisition procedure. The Court distinguished it from the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, which provided for acquisition for companies: under the challenged law the State acquired land for public purposes, whereas under the general law acquisition was at a company’s instance and for its benefit. No earlier cases are relied on in the supplied judgment.

predicates.procedural_discrimination_challenge_to_l: The proceeding alleges that different procedures for acquiring land under two legal schemes are procedurally discriminatory.
predicates.special_law_targets_planned_industrial_d: One scheme is specially directed to planned industrial development and has its own acquisition procedure.
predicates.state_acquires_for_public_purpose: Under the special scheme, the State acquires land for a public purpose rather than to fulfil a company’s acquisition request.
predicates.general_procedure_serves_company_at_its_: The other scheme permits acquisition initiated by and for the benefit of a company.

issues.definition: When a discrimination challenge compares acquisition procedures for planned public industrial development with a procedure for company-benefit acquisition, the differing procedures are not procedurally discriminatory.

issues.legal_issue: A requirement for government approval before a collector determines compensation above a specified amount does not restrict the collector’s compensation-determination power when the collector must apply compensation principles and a court can finally determine the amount.
material_facts: The acquisition law required government approval before the Collector could determine compensation above an amount specified by general order.
The law directed the Collector to be guided by sections 23 and 24 and other relevant provisions of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, when determining compensation.
The judgment found that the Government had fixed no ceiling on compensation.
An appeal from the Collector’s decision lay to a court, whose decision would finally determine the compensation.
issues.conclusion: The approval requirement did not restrict the Collector’s power to determine compensation; the Court’s appellate determination would finally settle the amount.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 33(3) and its proviso, prior government approval was required in the stated circumstances; section 33(5) required the Collector to be guided by sections 23 and 24 and other relevant provisions of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894. The absence of a government-fixed ceiling and the availability of an appeal to a court meant that the Collector’s compensation-determination power was not restricted. No earlier cases are relied on in the supplied judgment.

rule.if: challenge_to_compensation_approval_requirement and collector_applies_compensation_principles and no_government_ceiling_is_fixed and court_can_finally_determine_compensation

predicates.challenge_to_compensation_approval_requi: The proceeding challenges a requirement for government approval before a collector determines compensation above a specified amount.
predicates.collector_applies_compensation_principle: The collector is directed to determine compensation by reference to established compensation principles.
predicates.no_government_ceiling_is_fixed: The government has not fixed a ceiling on the compensation the collector may determine.
predicates.court_can_finally_determine_compensation: A court may review the collector’s decision and finally determine the compensation amount.

issues.definition: When a challenged approval requirement operates alongside compensation principles, no fixed government ceiling, and a court’s power to finally determine compensation, the requirement does not restrict compensation-determination power.
